summary:
Perlis stands under Malaysia's federal framework: the Penal Code 1936 applies in the state without modification. Sections 377A and 377B punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" for any person regardless of gender or consent, with acts of gross indecency criminalised alongside them, carrying up to 20 years' imprisonment and whipping. These offences are not limited to Malaysian nationals. The Human Dignity Trust's Malaysia country profile, last updated 16 December 2025, records them in force.

Perlis is one of all 13 states, together with Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya, that maintains Sharia enactments criminalising cross-dressing or "a man posing as a woman", with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. Since the 1980s every state has passed such an enactment, and three also bar women from posing as men. These state offences reach Muslims only. A non-Muslim foreign visitor in Perlis is not exposed to them; a Muslim visitor is, and enforcement rests with the state Islamic religious department.

No legal gender-recognition procedure is recorded for Malaysia, so a visitor whose identity documents do not match their presentation has no domestic process available to align them. Discrimination and violence against LGBT people are regularly reported in the country, and transgender people are documented as particularly vulnerable.

The national framework has been applied through raids and public proceedings since the 2018 election. An October 2022 raid on a Queer Halloween party in Kuala Lumpur produced at least 20 LGBT arrests; a raid on an LGBT venue in August drew twenty men; a Terengganu Sharia court ordered a lesbian couple caned; and in November 2023 Johor authorities announced plans for conversion-therapy centres. Raid operations have publicly identified detainees. None of the sources names a Perlis-specific enforcement case, so what a visitor faces here is the national pattern rather than a documented local record.

For a non-Muslim foreign visitor the operative exposure in Perlis is the federal Penal Code and venue-based raids. Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted; the documented pattern is raid-based arrest and public outing rather than individual stops.
tangentialFactors:
Human Rights Watch, with the Malaysian organisation Justice for Sisters, published "I Don't Want to Change Myself — Anti-LGBT Conversion Practices, Discrimination, and Violence in Malaysia" on 10 August 2022. Its 73 interviews with LGBT people across Malaysia conducted between 2018 and 2021 supply the evidentiary base for the national picture that governs Perlis, and the report names no Perlis-specific enforcement case.

The crackdown documented by the Human Dignity Trust since the 2018 election is dispersed across states and venues rather than concentrated in any one place, which means a visitor's exposure depends more on being present at a targeted venue than on which state they are in. Johor's November 2023 conversion-therapy plans and the Terengganu caning sentence sit alongside the Penal Code exposure as markers of official hostility rather than as provisions a visitor would be charged under.
localsOnly:
Government-run "rehabilitation" programmes are a fixture of life for LGBT residents: at least 1,733 people had attended them as of June 2021, according to the Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters report.

Residents who are Muslim fall under the state Sharia cross-dressing offence in addition to the federal Penal Code, with enforcement carried out by the state Islamic religious department and penalties reaching three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. Residents who are not Muslim face only the federal provisions.

No legal gender-recognition procedure is recorded, so residents seeking to align identity documents with their gender have no domestic route. The Human Dignity Trust records discrimination and violence against LGBT people as regularly reported, with transgender people particularly vulnerable.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory records a Perlis-specific enforcement case, arrest or court proceeding. The state's profile rests on the federal framework and on national patterns; whether Perlis authorities have used the cross-dressing offence recently is not sourced here.

The inventory contains no information on facilities, healthcare access or partner recognition for Perlis. Whether Perlis has carried out caning under its cross-dressing provision in the current period is also not sourced, and the penalty range is drawn from the national pattern rather than from a Perlis sentencing record.

The Human Dignity Trust profile is written at country level and does not itemise Perlis separately, so statements about raid frequency and venue targeting are national findings applied to the state.
